newsitem.title: RUSSIA: World market could handle Russia loans - analysts.
newsitem.headline: World market could handle Russia loans - analysts.

text.p: If President Boris Yeltsin really is looking for more money from the West to help to pay mounting Russian wage arrears, the international market is unlikely to turn him down, bankers said on Friday.
Such a move by the cash-strapped Russian government is by no means certain and confusion surrounded exactly what Yeltsin said on Friday.

Itar-Tass news agency quoted him as saying that Russia might turn to the leaders of foreign countries to ask for help in paying wage arrears to public sector employees such as teachers and doctors. He wanted to pay them by October.
"Let's turn to the leaders of foreign countries," Tass quoted him as telling Russian regional leaders.

But the Kremlin later issued a denial, saying in a statement: "This information does not correspond to reality." Tass gave no immediate explanation and television footage of the meeting did not include the remark.

This would not be the first time that the Kremlin has had to deny an off-the-cuff remark by Yeltsin. Even before the denial it was not clear whether he might have meant more borrowing from international finance organisations, from countries or on the world markets.
On the other hand, Russia has used some of the proceeds of a past international bond issue to fund pension arrears.
Speaking before the denial was issued, analysts said that if Russia were to borrow from the international market, the outlook was good.
"I think there continues to be good appetite for Russian paper," Morgan Stanley Vice President Eric Fine told Reuters.

"Russia as a creditor is basically underindebted and given the fact that the overall market seems to be constructive I do not see why further capital raising would be a big problem. I think they can raise more money."
It is not clear how big the state debt to public sector employees is, but wage arrears to the military alone appear to total at least five trillion roubles ($860 million).
Nikolai Klekovkin, deputy CEO at Credit Suisse Asset Management, said the price of foreign borrowing might be around nine to 11 percent annually.
"Of course, it will depend on what volume Russia wants to place," he said. "The international market will be able to digest $2-$3 billion without strong price fluctuations."
Russia has recently placed $2 billion in its third Eurobond, a 10-year issue at 375 basis points over U.S. Treasuries.
Russian government officials said the state had used part of the proceeds to pay pension arrears and said the next Eurobond would be issued in the autumn.
At that stage Russia expects to get an improved credit rating, which is now slightly lower than investment grade at BB- from Standard & Poor's and Ba2 from Moody's.
Analysts said Russia could count on getting an investment grade rating in the autumn.
Fine said that as Russia's fundamentals were improving, the capital available was becoming cheaper. "Between now and the next six months the borrowing cost is going down," he said.
